questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to have an authentic American college campus experience, and Cornell University was the perfect choice for that since it was located in a small town, Ithaca, where the university and its students made up the majority of residents.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had an amazing experience and made friendships and connections which I still keep in touch with.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, the coordinator for exchange students, Jess Hawkey, was very well organized and very helpful and gave us all the necessary information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had an orientation day for all the exchange students in August before the semester started where we recieved all the practical information as well as some useful cultural tips for our stay at Cornell.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Although I did hear of some exchange students who managed to get on campus housing, the vast majority of exchange students had to find off-campus housing. The coordinator helped us connect with local landlords to find a suitable rental property, and I managed to find an appartment north of Campus called Lakeland Appartments by Travis Hyde which was decent value for money and located in a nice area. I was connected with two other Danish students and a German as we were all searching for a place to stay and it worked our well. We were able to get a contract for only 6 months, which was nice as we were only staying there for the semester. I can't say Travis Hyde was the most well-organized landlord, as it was slightly difficult at times to communicate with them, but that said, we didn't experience any major issues and the appartment was good value for money when compared with some of the other options which other exchanges students were staying at.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: VERY IMPORTANT: make sure to live either in Collegetown or on North Campus as these are nice areas where lots of other students live. Do not live in the main town of Ithaca as it is down hill from campus and will make getting to campus very inconveniant, and it is not nearly as nice an area as either North campus or collegetown. In general just try to find something as close to campus as possible.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Course registration was quite conveniant.  If courses required prerequisites, you could email the professor directly and enquire about whether the course would be suitable or not, and in general the professors were very willing to help and I experienced no problems in getting the courses I wanted. At Cornell, there is a 3 week period where you can basically attend lectures and if you don't find the courses interesting or relevant you can still enroll in other courses and drop out of courses without it being registered on your transcript. This also means that if a course is full and you cant pre-enroll, you may still be able to enroll in the course as some other students may drop out of it in this period. In general, it never hurts to reach out to the professor and ask if there is space on a course, as often you will get a yes.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was a website where you could search for courses available in the semester and see if it was compatible with your timetable, i.e. that the courses didn't overlap with each other. This was very helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was able to get all of the courses I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Figure out the courses you might want to take in advance and remember to pre-enroll so you are guaranteed a spot. Thereafter, if there are other courses which might seem interesting, go to a lecture or two and perhaps you might want to enroll during the drop-period.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Two of the courses I took, were courses which were combined courses for both BA and MA students. The courses had different official names, however the lectures were the same. The only difference was that sometimes the MA students had to do slightly more challenging questions in asssignments or perhaps had more questions on the exam. Aside from that, it was the same course. Coming exchange students should be aware of this, as they may wish to consider whether to take the BA version of the course or the MA version, depending on how much they wish to challenge themselves. 

In terms of the academic level, it was perhaps slightly lower than what I am used to studying Mat-Øk at the Maths Institute at KU, however there was more work than at KU. In most courses, your grade was comprised of assignments, preliminary tests and a final exam, which meant you had to follow along and perform well throughout the course if you wanted to get a good grade. As opposed to at KU, where in many courses your grade is determined solely by your final exam.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was very similar; a combination of lectures and practice lessons (labs), where older students who had already taken the course were instructors.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
It is impossible for me to recommend specific courses as it totally depends on the interests of the student. 
While I didn't take it myself, I knew many people who took "Wine Tasting" as a course, which sounded like a lot of fun :)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: We had to have a mandatory insurance which cost 1200 USD. Groceries were also more expensive than I expected. I ended up buying a meal plan (they can be quite expensive) so that I could eat on campus, since the food was actually very good and we lived quite far away from the nearest supermarket, so shopping was a bit inconveniant.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: You could use all of the local buses in Ithaca for free with your student ID card.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The non-academic opportunities were endless. There were countless clubs suiting whatever interests you might have. For me personally, I joined the Club Tennis team, as I am quite an avid tennis player, and I also joined the running club quite often as the nature is really beautiful in Ithaca. There is an official club day fair where you can explore all of the clubs and find something that interests you. There are also many speaker events by esteemed academics or heads of industry.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: See answer to previous question.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The running club is a great way to meet new people and explore the area. You don't have to be a good runner at all, as there is always a social pace run where people chat and have fun.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: The obvious choice is to spend some time in NYC as it is only a approx 4.5 hour bus ride away from Ithaca and it is an amazing city (though expensive). Personally, me and some other exchange students rented some cars and drove to Quebec, Canada over the thanksgiving break, which was a lot of fun. There is a small local airport which flies to NYC, so some more adventurous people travelled further over the fall break. Niagara falls is also only abour 2.5 hours away, howeveer it isnt worth more than a day trip as the city itself isnt that interesting.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. People were very welcoming and open. It is a very international/diverse crowd of people who attend Cornell, so it barely feels like you are a foreigner in that environment.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join clubs, and attend any official school events. Eating at the dining halls for lunch or dinner is also a great way to meet new people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There was nothing which I found particularly challenging.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How open-minded and easy people were to talk to, as well as how driven and intelligent many of the students were.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. If you are living off-campus, make sure to stay either near North campus (Cayuga Heights) or in Collegetown (south of campus), just dont stay in downtown Ithaca (west of campus) 
2. I would recommend getting some form of meal plan, as the food in the dining halls, in particular Morrison dining hall (the newest one) is actually really good, and I have some of my fondest memories eating dinner with friends there. 
3. Enjoy the nature and explore the local area.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of the social life also revolves around fraternitites and sororities, so it may be worthwile making some friends who are members of "greek life" if you are interested in partying etc.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Making friends with so many interesting people, both Americans and other exchange students from different parts of the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Leaving Cornell :)

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
